issues.legal_issue: Priority by filing date does not prevent competing pending applications for mining leases from being considered together on their comparative merits.
material_facts: Several applications for leases over overlapping mineral-bearing areas remained pending at different stages while additional applicants entered the proceedings.
The statutory scheme did not clearly identify which applications for an area should be considered together, and delay had allowed the number of competing claims to grow.
The Court considered that national mineral development required selection of the best-qualified applicants or distribution among applicants capable of efficient exploitation.
issues.conclusion: The earliest application does not automatically determine entitlement; all applications pending for consideration when the decision is made should be considered together. The Court also said that clearer statutory guidelines and a time-bound procedure for defined areas were needed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(2) states a general preference based on the earlier application, but section 11(4) permits an out-of-turn grant for recorded special reasons with prior Central Government approval. Read as a whole, section 11 does not compel a grant solely by filing order. National interest and efficient exploitation support comparative consideration of pending applications. Ferro Alloys Corporation of India v. Union and Mysore Cements Ltd. v. Union were distinguished because they did not establish that an earlier application must be granted without considering later pending applications.

predicates.mining_lease_case: The proceeding concerns competing claims for a lease to mine a mineral.
predicates.competing_applications_pending: More than one application concerning the same or overlapping area is pending when the authority considers the claims.
predicates.comparative_selection_needed: The circumstances call for selecting the applicants best able to exploit the mineral efficiently or distributing the area among capable applicants.

issues.definition: When a mining-lease case involves competing pending applications and comparative selection is needed, the applications are considered together rather than decided solely by filing order.

issues.legal_issue: The challenged reservation policy for mineral-bearing areas was not shown to be arbitrary or mala fide.
material_facts: The State had adopted a policy of reserving mineral-bearing areas for public-sector exploitation and had notified the reservation.
The State had generally adhered to the reservation policy, subject to a small number of exceptional grants or relaxations.
The policy changes were explained by mineral conservation and development considerations, and the record did not substantiate arbitrariness or bad faith.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the reservation policy against the challenge of arbitrariness and mala fides.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the reservation power under rule 58 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, and relied on Venkataraman v. Union in addressing the allegation of malice in law. It held that conservation and proper utilisation of an important mineral were legitimate considerations and that the record did not establish arbitrary or mala fide policy-making.

predicates.challenge_to_mining_reservation_policy: A party challenges a government policy reserving mineral-bearing areas for exploitation in the public sector.
predicates.mineral_conservation_interest: The government relies on conservation and proper utilisation of an important mineral as a reason for the reservation policy.
predicates.no_evidence_of_arbitrary_policy: The record does not substantiate that the government formulated or applied the policy arbitrarily or in bad faith.

issues.definition: A reservation policy challenged in a mining case is not invalidated as arbitrary when conservation is a relevant interest and the record does not substantiate arbitrary or bad-faith action.

issues.legal_issue: A private lease over a duly reserved area requires lawful dereservation or a justified relaxation of the reservation restriction.
material_facts: The relevant areas had been reserved for public-sector exploitation by notification.

The areas had not been made available for grant through the required notification process, and the Central Government had not made a written, reasoned relaxation for the private applicants as a general matter.
The Court recognised that a private grant could nevertheless be possible if the area were lawfully opened for applications or the Central Government relaxed the restriction for recorded reasons.
issues.conclusion: A lease to a private applicant could not be granted unless the area was dereserved and opened to applications or the Central Government, after considering the State’s recommendations, recorded reasons for a justified relaxation.
issues.legal_principle: Rules 58, 59(1) and 59(2) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 governed reservation, availability for grant, and relaxation. Section 17A of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 addressed statutory reservations. The Court relied on Amritlal Nathubhai Shah v. Union of India in recognising the validity of the reservation power. A reserved area is unavailable for grant unless the applicable notification requirements are met or the Central Government relaxes the restriction for recorded reasons.

rule.if: private_mining_lease_case and area_reserved and not area_lawfully_opened and not justified_central_relaxation

predicates.private_mining_lease_case: The proceeding concerns a private applicant seeking a mining lease.
predicates.area_reserved: The area has been reserved for public-sector exploitation or another legally recognised reservation purpose.
predicates.not area_lawfully_opened: The area has not been lawfully dereserved and opened for applications.
predicates.not justified_central_relaxation: The Central Government has not justified and recorded a relaxation permitting the proposed private grant.

issues.definition: A private mining lease is unavailable while the area remains reserved and neither lawful opening for applications nor a justified Central Government relaxation has occurred.

issues.legal_issue: A public-sector corporation has no statutory entitlement to insist that a reserved mining area be leased exclusively to it or to veto a private grant.
material_facts: Two State-controlled corporations relied on the reservation of areas for public-sector exploitation to claim leases to the exclusion of private applicants.
The reservation was general and did not itself confer rights on those corporations.
The State could choose how reserved areas were exploited, could dereserve an area, or could seek a Central Government relaxation permitting a private lease.
issues.conclusion: The corporations could not insist that leases be granted only to them or object to a private grant solely on the basis of the reservation; allocation to a public-sector entity remained for the State to decide.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied rules 58 and 59 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 and section 17A of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. A general reservation for public-sector exploitation does not directly confer a right to a lease on a particular public-sector corporation. The State retains discretion among public-sector entities, and the reservation does not prevent a private grant where the area is lawfully opened or the Central Government relaxes the restriction.

predicates.public_sector_corporation_claims_exclusi: A public-sector corporation claims that a reserved area must be leased to it and no other applicant.
predicates.reservation_is_general: The reservation identifies public-sector exploitation generally rather than granting a specific corporation an entitlement.
predicates.state_can_choose_exploiter: The State retains authority to choose the public-sector entity that will exploit the area or to pursue lawful opening or relaxation.

issues.definition: A public-sector corporation cannot demand an exclusive lease or veto a private grant merely because an area is generally reserved for public-sector exploitation.

issues.legal_issue: A preliminary government recommendation that a mining lease be granted does not create promissory estoppel when the required higher-level approval was never given.
material_facts: The State had at one stage recommended that a private applicant receive a lease over part of the area sought.
The proposed grant required Central Government approval, which was never given.
The State later dealt with the application in light of Central Government directions and the reservation policy.
issues.conclusion: The preliminary recommendation did not prevent the State from disposing of the application in light of the governing directions, and no ground for promissory estoppel was made out.
issues.legal_principle: The Court referred to Kanai Lal Sur v. Paramnidhi Sadhukhan, Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat State Financial Corporation v. Lotus Hotels, Surya Narain Yadav v. Bihar State Electricity Board, Godfrey Philips India Ltd. v. Union of India, and Mahabir Auto Stores v. Indian Oil Corporation. On the facts, the Court held that a State recommendation was insufficient where the required Central Government approval had not been obtained.

predicates.mining_lease_case: The proceeding concerns an application for a mining lease.
predicates.state_made_preliminary_recommendation: The State recommended or proposed that the applicant receive a lease but had not completed the grant.
predicates.required_higher_approval_absent: An approval required from a higher government authority was never given.

issues.definition: A preliminary State recommendation does not create an estoppel against later disposal of a mining application when required higher-level approval was absent.

issues.legal_issue: A court-referred report by a Central Government officer could be treated as the Central Government’s decision on the competing mining claims.
material_facts: The Court referred the competing claims pending on a specified date to the Secretary in the Central Government’s mines department for consideration.
The officer considered the parties’ claims and submitted findings after the Court directed that the claims be examined.
The referral was intended to secure an effective decision on the claims, and the officer was authorised to deal with the matter.
issues.conclusion: Although styled a report, the officer’s findings were in the nature of a Central Government decision on the parties’ claims and could be reviewed on their merits by the Court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the referral and the officer’s findings as an exercise of the Central Government’s revisional decision-making function under section 30 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. It found no procedural defect in the specially directed process, noting that the statute and rules did not require the internal tribunal arrangement relied on by the objectors and that the officer was authorised to consider the claims.

predicates.court_referred_competing_mining_claims_t: A court refers competing claims for mineral leases to an officer in the Central Government’s responsible department.
predicates.officer_was_authorised: The officer is authorised to consider and decide the referred claims.
predicates.officer_considered_claims: The officer considers the parties’ claims and submits findings on them.

issues.definition: When an authorised Central Government officer considers claims referred by the court, the resulting report may be treated as the government’s decision on those claims.

issues.legal_issue: Mining grants supported by adequate case-specific reasons and an applicable relaxation of reservation could be upheld despite the general reservation policy.
material_facts: The State had agreed to grant leases to three applicants, including an individual who had discovered and previously worked the mineral deposit and companies with identified industrial requirements.
The grants were made in the context of the litigation and were supported by material concerning prior operations, the applicants’ needs, and the areas granted.
The Central Government’s approval or relaxation was reflected in the grant process or in the decision affirming the proposed grant.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the grants to the two companies and upheld the decision concerning the individual’s lease, directing the State to execute that lease.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied rule 59(2) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, under which the Central Government could relax the restriction on the availability of reserved areas for recorded special reasons. It held that the grants could be sustained on the case-specific reasons shown by the records and litigation materials, notwithstanding the absence of elaborate reasons in the original grant orders.

rule.if: mining_lease_grant_challenged and reservation_applies and case_specific_reasons_support_grant and relaxation_approved_or_inferred

predicates.mining_lease_grant_challenged: A party challenges a grant or agreed grant of a mining lease.
predicates.reservation_applies: The area is subject to a reservation that restricts its availability for grant.
predicates.case_specific_reasons_support_grant: The record supports the grant through relevant circumstances such as prior operations, discovery, or demonstrated industrial requirements.
predicates.relaxation_approved_or_inferred: The required relaxation or approval is evidenced by the grant process or can fairly be inferred from the decision-making record.

issues.definition: A challenged mining grant may be upheld despite reservation when relevant case-specific reasons support it and the required relaxation or approval is established.

issues.legal_issue: A summary rejection of mining-lease claims that does not address the applicants’ relevant grounds cannot stand and requires fresh consideration.
material_facts: Two applicants sought leases and presented grounds concerning their mineral requirements, industrial operations, supply difficulties, and other circumstances relevant to whether an exception to the reservation policy was justified.
The officer rejected their claims without addressing the various considerations they had raised.
The State had not previously considered those claims in the relevant light.
issues.conclusion: The rejection of the two claims was set aside, and the applications were restored for fresh consideration by the State Government.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the rejection was too cryptic and unsustainable because it did not address the material considerations raised. The State was required to consider the relevant factors bearing on whether a lease could be granted as an exception to its reservation policy; the Court expressed no conclusion on whether either applicant ultimately qualified.

predicates.mining_lease_claim_rejected: An authority has rejected an application for a mining lease.
predicates.applicant_raised_relevant_material_facto: The applicant presented material considerations relevant to the merits of the lease claim or a possible exception to reservation.
predicates.decision_omitted_those_factors: The decision did not address the material considerations raised by the applicant.

issues.definition: A mining-lease rejection is set aside for fresh consideration when the applicant raised relevant factors that the decision-maker failed to address.
